name: Ceramide oral (wheat)

lead:
Ceramides are lipids that help hold the skin barrier together and keep water in. Oral ceramide supplements use plant sources, often wheat, to supply ceramide-type lipids by mouth, with the aim of improving dryness and skin texture.
Trials of oral plant glycosylceramides are small; one six-week randomized study of a konjac extract reported less dryness, redness and oiliness. Studies of wheat-sourced products specifically are not among the published trials listed here.

paras: Taken daily as capsules or tablets, often in beauty-supplement blends with hyaluronic acid, collagen or antioxidants. Users commonly report waiting several weeks before judging skin changes, and pair it with a topical moisturizer.

Adverse effects in the small trials were not a feature; the main caution is for people with wheat or gluten allergy or celiac disease, who check product sourcing and labelling. Supplement quality and ceramide content vary between brands.

chain: Plant ceramides taken daily by mouth
Skin barrier lipids and hydration support
Less dryness, smoother skin tone and texture
angle.text: People take oral wheat ceramide to support the skin's moisture barrier from within, aiming for plumper, less dry skin. Results in trials were measured over weeks.

lead: Oral ceramide supplements supply plant-derived ceramides, such as those extracted from wheat, as capsules or powders. Ceramides are a major lipid of the skin barrier, and low ceramide content has been linked with dry, rough skin, which is the reasoning behind taking them by mouth.[1]

A 2020 randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 51 volunteers gave a konjac tuber extract standardized to glycosylceramides for six weeks and reported significant improvements in dryness, hyperpigmentation, redness, itching and oiliness.[1] A 2016 trial of a zeaxanthin-based oral and topical regimen that included phytoceramides reported better hydration and fewer wrinkles, though the product was a multi-ingredient combination.[2]
The konjac findings are from a different plant; wheat-specific oral ceramide studies are lacking.

paras: Ceramides are sphingolipids that sit in the outer skin layer. Laboratory work on model skin lipid membranes examines how ceramide types such as phytosphingosine ceramides affect permeability and structure.[3] Oral plant extracts are marketed as glucosylceramides or phytoceramides.

The konjac glycosylceramide trial reported improvements on dermatologist-assessed dryness and self-assessed measures after six weeks.[1] The zeaxanthin and phytoceramide combination trial reported improved hydration and fewer wrinkles but cannot isolate the ceramide.[2]
Product labels advise people with wheat or gluten sensitivity to check the source. Content and purity vary between brands.

A randomized placebo-controlled trial of 51 adults using a konjac extract (about 5 mg glycosylceramides per day) for six weeks reported significant improvement in dryness, pigmentation, redness, itching and oiliness.[1] A randomized trial of a multi-ingredient oral and topical product including phytoceramides reported improvements in hydration and wrinkle count in women.[2] No studies of wheat-derived oral ceramide specifically are known.
